title: Reynolds-number-dependent entrance bias in temperature polarization of lab-scale membrane distillation
authors: Soyoung Kim, Tiezheng Tong, Yinuo Noah Yao
abstract: Lab-scale membrane distillation (MD) modules are commonly used for membrane characterization and developing empirical heat-transfer correlations. Entrance-induced flow structures can introduce geometry-specific effects into measured temperature polarization (TP) and heat transfer. However, the dependence of these effects on module geometry and flow condition remains unclear. We performed three-dimensional computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations of direct contact membrane distillation (DCMD) over inlet Reynolds numbers of $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}=10$-$1000$, focusing on side-chamber length and main-channel height. We discovered that counter-rotating streamwise vortices formed near the main-channel entrance across all geometries, but their downstream persistence increased with $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}$. At lower $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}$, the vortices mostly decayed before mid-channel, while at higher $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}$ they persisted farther downstream and produced pronounced spatial variations in TP. Increasing side-chamber length reduced the secondary-flow kinetic energy entering the main channel, and generally strengthened TP, whereas increasing main-channel height reduced the bulk velocity and streamwise kinetic energy, resulting in a thicker thermal boundary layer and stronger TP. For most geometries, the deviation from the straight-channel baseline changed from stronger TP at lower $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}$ to weaker TP at higher $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}$. Entrance effects therefore vary in both magnitude and direction with operating condition and cannot be represented by a constant correction across the Reynolds-number range.

infographic.key_insight: Entrance effects in lab-scale DCMD are Reynolds-number dependent: near-inlet vortices can either strengthen or weaken temperature polarization depending on flow rate and geometry.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Membrane distillation module design and heat-transfer correlations must account for entrance geometry and operating Reynolds number, rather than using a single constant correction.
method: 3D CFD of direct contact membrane distillation modules
Sweep of inlet Reynolds number from 10 to 1000
Varied side-chamber length and main-channel height to isolate geometry effects
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations showed counter-rotating streamwise vortices near the entrance across all geometries, with persistence and TP deviation increasing at higher Reynolds numbers and changing sign relative to a straight-channel baseline.
infographic.watch_item: Because the entrance bias changes with both geometry and Reynolds number, corrections calibrated at one operating condition may not transfer reliably to others.
infographic.paper_title: Reynolds-number-dependent entrance bias in temperature polarization of lab-scale membrane distillation

title: High-fidelity Three-Dimensional Flow Field Reconstruction Driven by Turbulent Fluid Dynamics
authors: Hanlin Kong, Jianan Wei, Yuntian Chen, Yujia Wang, Wenguan Wang
abstract: High-fidelity three-dimensional turbulent flow fields are essential for scientific and engineering analyses, yet obtaining them through direct numerical simulation or high-resolution measurements remains expensive. Super-resolution reconstruction from coarse-grained data therefore offers a promising alternative, but remains fundamentally challenging because fine-scale structures are intrinsically three-dimensional and dynamically coupled across scales. Existing data-driven approaches still struggle to recover multiscale volumetric structures and their coherent temporal evolution. To address these limitations, we propose a turbulence-aware framework for time-resolved three-dimensional flow reconstruction. The framework couples a multiscale neural operator, designed to recover volumetric structures, with a state space model to promote temporal consistency in the reconstructed dynamics. In addition, Navier-Stokes residuals are incorporated as soft constraints to regularize the reconstruction toward physically plausible dynamics. A mixture-of-experts mechanism is also introduced to support unsupervised adaptation to unknown coarse-graining. Across evaluations on canonical turbulent systems and atmospheric reanalysis data, the proposed framework reduces reconstruction errors relative to learning-based and classical baselines, while better preserving multiscale spatial structure and coherent temporal evolution. These results validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in reconstructing high-fidelity three-dimensional flow fields from coarse-grained data.

infographic.key_insight: A turbulence-aware reconstruction pipeline can recover high-fidelity 3D flow fields from coarse data by combining multiscale spatial decoding, temporal state-space modeling, and physics-based regularization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This could enable cheaper access to volumetric turbulent flow estimates for CFD analysis, design optimization, and atmospheric monitoring when direct simulation or dense measurements are impractical.
method: Multiscale neural operator reconstructs fine 3D volumetric structures from coarse-grained inputs.
State space model enforces coherent time evolution in the reconstructed dynamics.
Navier-Stokes residuals and a mixture-of-experts module add physics guidance and adapt to unknown coarse-graining.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports lower reconstruction error than learning-based and classical baselines on canonical turbulent systems and atmospheric reanalysis data, while better preserving multiscale structure and temporal coherence.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on the quality of physics residuals and the model’s ability to generalize across different coarse-graining patterns and flow regimes.
infographic.paper_title: High-fidelity Three-Dimensional Flow Field Reconstruction Driven by Turbulent Fluid Dynamics

title: Component-wise outer similarity of turbulent boundary layers with strong adverse-pressure gradient
authors: Yu-Xuan Shi, Mingze Ma, Xi Chen
abstract: The adverse-pressure-gradient (APG) effect challenges the classical scaling of turbulent boundary layers (TBLs) over a flat plate, and it remains unclear whether outer-layer similarity holds across a wide range of APG strengths.We assemble a benchmark comprising the present direct numerical simulation of a suction--blowing-induced separation bubble and published profiles, spanning Clauser parameters $β_e=0.04$--$180$ and Reynolds numbers $Re_θ=530$--$19000$. Across this broad $(β_e,Re_θ)$ parameter range, existing APG normalizations do not simultaneously collapse the two mean-velocity defects and four Reynolds-stress components, leaving open whether outer similarity persists. Instead of defining new scalings, we normalize each quantity by its value at a common location $y_s$. Results are shown using $y_s=0.5δ$, beyond the outer stress peaks. For each of the six quantities, the normalized profiles exhibit a common outer shape across the conditions, with collapse emerging for $y/δ\gtrsim0.2$ for the velocity defects and $y/δ\gtrsim0.4$ for the Reynolds stresses. The collapse-error analysis shows that outer self-similarity is retained over a broad range of $y_s$ within the outer region and is not restricted to $y_s=0.5δ$. Furthermore, explicit expressions are provided for the normalized outer profiles. These results support component-wise outer similarity under strong APGs and provide compact references for APG turbulence-model assessment and conditional profile reconstruction.

infographic.key_insight: Under strong adverse-pressure gradients, the outer parts of turbulent boundary-layer profiles still collapse when each component is normalized by its value at a common outer location, indicating component-wise outer similarity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides compact outer-profile references for turbulence model validation and conditional reconstruction in APG boundary layers, including near separation conditions.
method: Built a benchmark from new DNS of a suction–blowing-induced separation bubble plus published APG profiles.
Tested six quantities: two mean-velocity defects and four Reynolds-stress components across wide b2_e and Re_b8 ranges.
Normalized each profile by its value at a shared outer point y_s (shown with y_s = 0.5b4) and checked profile collapse and error trends.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across b2_e = 0.04 180 and Re_b8 = 530 19000, the authors report outer collapse for all six quantities, with velocity defects collapsing for y/b4  0.2 and Reynolds stresses for y/b4  0.4.
infographic.watch_item: The collapse is component-wise and depends on choosing an outer reference location y_s, so it should not be treated as a universal inner-layer scaling or assumed to hold unchanged near the wall.
infographic.paper_title: Component-wise outer similarity of turbulent boundary layers with strong adverse-pressure gradient

title: Some generalizations of the tornado model
authors: S. N. Artekha
abstract: A possible mechanism of tornado generation is associated with the Schwarzschild criterion for convective instability. The supercooled cloud-air mixture near the axis starts to descend and, due to the super adiabatic temperature gradient, the overheated near-surface air mass rises. The complete system of equations for full model includes equations for the stream function, for the azimuthal velocity component, and for the change in density. The refined model considers rotating convection within the framework of ideal hydrodynamics. The simplest model uses a separate equation for the stream function and can be applied to the initial stage of vortex generation. Within the framework of the simplest model, an analytical solution is combined from 8 linear dependencies by height. Rotation increases due to the conservation of angular momentum. Within the framework of the refined model, some unidirectional differential rotation arises, but it depends on boundary conditions (can be local). The full model studies the tornado development as rotating convection from the very beginning to the quasi-stationary stage. Velocity components increase in a coordinated manner. Two cases are considered: a single whirlwind and a two-eyed tornado. Radial flows converge towards the central part of the tornado near the earth surface, and there is an outflow from the "wall" to the axis and to the periphery near the top of the tornado. The maximum vertical velocity component is achieved at a certain radial distance at a certain height. The maximum azimuthal velocity component is achieved in the tornado "wall". Tornado generation criteria are discussed.

infographic.key_insight: The paper frames tornado formation as rotating convection driven by convective instability, with angular-momentum conservation amplifying rotation and shaping the vortex from initiation to quasi-stationary development.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It provides a hierarchy of tornado models that can help researchers analyze vortex genesis, circulation structure, and velocity extrema relevant to severe-weather dynamics and CFD simplifications.
method: Builds a full hydrodynamic model using equations for stream function, azimuthal velocity, and density change.
Introduces a refined ideal-hydrodynamics model for rotating convection with boundary-condition-dependent differential rotation.
Uses a simplest stream-function model with an analytical solution assembled from 8 linear height dependencies to describe early vortex formation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports model-based analysis of tornado criteria and velocity-structure predictions for single-whirlwind and two-eyed tornado cases, rather than experimental data or numerical validation.
infographic.watch_item: The refined and simplest models are sensitive to boundary conditions and idealized assumptions, so direct quantitative prediction of real tornadoes may be limited.
infographic.paper_title: Some generalizations of the tornado model

title: AI Meets Turbulence Modeling: Complex Systems Perspective
authors: Sharath S. Girimaji
abstract: Despite widespread enthusiasm, applying artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) to turbulence modeling has yielded only modest progress, primarily due to a lack of situation-aware deployment. Data-driven Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (ML-RANS) closures frequently fail to generalize across diverse flow regimes, while scale-resolving simulations (SRS) remain computationally prohibitive. As a result, ML-RANS is often misapplied outside its domain of validity, and ML-SRS is unnecessarily deployed on flows fully amenable to RANS. To guide optimal AI/ML deployment, we propose a turbulence taxonomy map parameterized by degrees of freedom ($Re$) and the degree of non-equilibrium ($SK/ε$). By applying Weaver's well-recognized complexity framework, we classify turbulence into distinct physical regimes. This categorization identifies where local ML-RANS surrogates can generalize, clarifies where explicit scale resolution is physically mandatory, and highlights where physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are most effective. Ultimately, this perspective establishes a physics-grounded framework for the flow-aware, successful deployment of AI/ML in turbulence.

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that AI/ML in turbulence modeling works best when matched to the flow’s regime, using a complexity map in Reynolds number and non-equilibrium to decide between ML-RANS, scale-resolving simulation, and PINNs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For CFD practice, this provides a physics-based deployment guide that can reduce wasted compute and prevent applying learned closures outside their valid flow domain.
method: Build a turbulence taxonomy map using degrees of freedom (Re) and non-equilibrium (SK/ε).
Apply Weaver’s complexity framework to separate flow regimes by physical complexity.
Use the map to match each regime to the appropriate modeling strategy: ML-RANS, SRS, or PINNs.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that prior AI/ML turbulence efforts have shown only modest progress, with ML-RANS often failing to generalize and SRS often being computationally prohibitive.
infographic.watch_item: The framework is conceptual rather than a new benchmarked algorithm, so its practical value depends on correctly diagnosing the flow regime before choosing a model.
infographic.paper_title: AI Meets Turbulence Modeling: Complex Systems Perspective

title: Extreme-Scale Super-Resolution of Homogeneous Turbulence from a Single Realization
authors: Arth Sojitra, Muhammad Abid, Omer San
abstract: Homogeneous turbulent flows exhibit recurring multiscale structures across spatially separated regions, suggesting that a single flow realization may contain sufficient information to learn representations of unresolved scales. We investigate this hypothesis through an extreme super-resolution framework in which a wide-activation deep super-resolution (WDSR) network is trained exclusively on overlapping patches extracted from a single high-resolution turbulent realization. Previously unseen flow fields are reconstructed through patchwise prediction followed by Hann-window-weighted overlap-add assembly. The framework is evaluated for two-dimensional homogeneous isotropic turbulence at super-resolution factors of x32 and x64, representing severe spatial under-resolution. Despite the limited training data, the proposed approach reconstructs coherent vortical structures and recovers fine-scale features more accurately than conventional interpolation. Spectral and statistical analyses further demonstrate improved recovery of high-wavenumber energy content and multiscale flow characteristics. To assess the effectiveness of exploiting internal spatial information, we compare the proposed framework against WDSR models trained on 1, 25, 50, and 100 complete high-resolution snapshots without patch extraction. This comparison distinguishes the benefits of localized learning from those associated with increasing the number of training realizations. The results demonstrate that exploiting spatial redundancy within a single turbulent realization enables accurate reconstruction of previously unseen flow fields, even under extreme spatial under-resolution. These findings establish single-realization patch-based learning as a promising data-efficient approach for turbulent super-resolution when high-resolution training data are scarce.

infographic.key_insight: A single high-resolution turbulent snapshot contains enough recurring spatial structure to train a super-resolution model that reconstructs unseen flow fields and fine-scale vortices.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests a data-efficient path for turbulence modeling and simulation enhancement when high-resolution DNS/experimental data are scarce or expensive.
method: Train a WDSR network only on overlapping patches from one high-resolution 2D homogeneous isotropic turbulence realization.
Predict unresolved patches and stitch them back together using Hann-window-weighted overlap-add.
Benchmark against interpolation and WDSR models trained on full snapshots at x32 and x64 super-resolution factors.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improved recovery of vortical structures, high-wavenumber energy, and multiscale statistics on previously unseen flow fields at extreme under-resolution.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on the degree of spatial redundancy in the flow and on careful patch assembly to avoid seam artifacts or bias from a single training realization.
infographic.paper_title: Extreme-Scale Super-Resolution of Homogeneous Turbulence from a Single Realization

title: Two-Way Coupled Dynamics of Quantized Vortex Bundle Formation in Spatially Periodic Normal-Fluid Turbulence
authors: Hiromichi Kobayashi, Makoto Tsubota, Rio Yokota
abstract: Using fully coupled two-way simulations combining the vortex filament model with the Navier--Stokes equations, we discover that quantized vortices in superfluid $^4$He are systematically rolled up into coherent bundles within normal-fluid vortex tubes. Although co-rotating quantized vortices do not aggregate spontaneously, mutual friction with the normal fluid actively drives their bundling, directly inheriting the spatial hierarchy of classical turbulence. Mutual friction excites high-wavenumber normal-fluid vortex tubes adjacent to quantized vortices, while the superfluid forms a nested structure of thick low-wavenumber outer tubes and fine high-wavenumber inner tubes around the vortex lines. A distinct time lag between superfluid kinetic energy and dissipation fuels the energy cascade, giving rise to Kolmogorov's $k^{-5/3}$ spectrum. Crucially, bundle lifetimes are governed by the ratio of the local coupling time scale $t_\mathrm{cl}$ to the Kolmogorov dissipation time scale $τ_η$ ($t_\mathrm{cl}/τ_η< 20$), leading to enhanced thermal stability at higher temperatures. These findings establish a unified mechanism for two-fluid multiscale vortex organization.

infographic.key_insight: Two-way coupling between superfluid vortices and normal-fluid turbulence actively rolls quantized vortices into coherent bundles, reproducing classical multiscale vortex organization and a Kolmogorov-like energy cascade.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The result clarifies how temperature-dependent mutual friction shapes vortex clustering and dissipation in superfluid helium, which is important for modeling cryogenic flow systems and quantum-turbulence devices.
method: Fully coupled vortex filament model with Navier--Stokes simulation
Imposed spatially periodic normal-fluid turbulence
Analyzed coupling time scales, energy lag, and spectra
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports simulated bundle formation, a distinct time lag between superfluid kinetic energy and dissipation, and emergence of a $k^{-5/3}$ spectrum, with bundle lifetimes tied to $t_\mathrm{cl}/\tau_\eta<20$.
infographic.watch_item: The conclusions depend on a specific two-way coupled numerical setup and periodic turbulence forcing, so transferability to other geometries or forcing conditions should be checked.
infographic.paper_title: Two-Way Coupled Dynamics of Quantized Vortex Bundle Formation in Spatially Periodic Normal-Fluid Turbulence

title: Numerical Modeling of a Metallic Alloy Droplet Impact, Solidification, and Macrosegregation
authors: Ehsan Amani, Ali Moinirad
abstract: For the first time, we study the effects of mass transfer on alloy droplet impact, solidification, and solute non-homogeneity or MacroSegregation (MS). For this purpose, a multi-physics model, including fully-coupled hydrodynamics of multiphase flow, wetting, conjugate heat transfer, phase change, and mass transfer, is established and validated carefully across several benchmarks. In addition, a concentration-flux-correction algorithm is proposed to conserve the solute mass within the droplet at the numerical discretization level. The validated model is subsequently used to explore the impact and solidification of an alloy droplet. The results show that accounting for mass transfer and solute transport improves the prediction of the dynamics of a solidifying splat, in a consistent manner with experimental observations, while this effect has been neglected in all previous studies. The analysis demonstrates that this improvement results from the flow sensitivity to the mushy region thickness, which is regulated by local solute concentration through the solidus and liquidus temperatures. Furthermore, analyses of the MS map identify several critical segregation regions most susceptible to defect initiation, such as cracking, including a long negatively segregated vein within the lamella, formed by the severe advective flow through the mush in the middle stages of the impact, a positively segregated region near the rim of the splat, appearing as a result of hook formation, and a major positively segregated zone at the top of the rim, which develops following the accumulation of the solute-rich melt sustained by washout from the lamella.

infographic.key_insight: Including solute transport and mass conservation changes predicted droplet impact and solidification behavior, because local composition alters mushy-zone thickness and thus the flow.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model improves prediction of alloy splat formation and segregation defects, helping guide additive manufacturing and coating processes where cracking risk matters.
method: Fully coupled multiphysics model for multiphase hydrodynamics, wetting, conjugate heat transfer, phase change, and mass transfer.
Concentration-flux-correction algorithm to conserve solute mass at the discretization level.
Validated against several benchmarks before simulating alloy droplet impact and macrosegregation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports careful benchmark validation and shows better agreement with experiments when mass transfer and solute transport are included.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy depends on resolving mushy-region physics and concentration transport; coarse grids or simplified solute models may miss segregation hotspots.
infographic.paper_title: Numerical Modeling of a Metallic Alloy Droplet Impact, Solidification, and Macrosegregation

title: eMOOD: Entropy-Based Multidimensional Optimal Order Detection for High-Order Shock-Capturing Finite-Volume Schemes
authors: Michał Umiński, Panagiotis Tsoutsanis, Ahmed A Sheikh Al-Shabab, Alan S. Dawes
abstract: We present eMOOD, an entropy-guided evolution of the Multidimensional Optimal Order Detection (MOOD) framework for high-order finite-volume methods on unstructured meshes. A novel troubled-cell indicator based on numerical entropy production replaces the classical relaxed discrete maximum principle. Using entropy generation as a physically motivated measure of non-smoothness, the detector targets shocks, contact discontinuities and under-resolved flow features with a compact stencil. Compared with conventional MOOD detection, eMOOD reduces flagged cells by up to 75%, improving efficiency and reducing memory-access overhead. The detector is used within both the classical MOOD cascade of progressively reduced-order schemes and a novel MOOD-CWENO hybrid, which retains inexpensive linear reconstruction in smooth regions and activates nonlinear high-order reconstruction only where needed. Implemented in the open-source parallel solver UCNS3D, the methodology is assessed on the Shu-Osher shock-entropy-wave interaction, double Mach reflection, supersonic forward-facing step, shock-helium-bubble interaction and triple material point problems. These benchmarks encompass strong shock interactions, shock-induced instabilities, multi-material interfaces and vortex-dominated flows, testing robustness, shock capturing and accuracy on unstructured meshes. Results show that eMOOD preserves the accuracy and robustness of reference CWENO and MOOD formulations while achieving speed-ups of up to 20% without loss of solution quality. Its compact detection stencil, reduced memory footprint and improved localisation offer a more scalable and efficient framework for massively parallel high-order compressible-flow simulations. infographic.key_insight: eMOOD replaces MOOD's classical troubled-cell test with entropy production, enabling more targeted shock detection in high-order finite-volume solvers.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method improves robustness and scalability for unstructured-mesh compressible-flow simulations by reducing unnecessary cell flagging, memory traffic, and runtime.
method: Uses numerical entropy generation as a compact-stencil troubled-cell indicator.
Integrates the detector into both a classical MOOD cascade and a MOOD-CWENO hybrid.
Activates nonlinear reconstruction only where entropy signals non-smooth flow.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across shock and multiphase benchmarks, eMOOD flagged up to 75% fewer cells and delivered speed-ups of up to 20% while maintaining solution quality.
infographic.watch_item: Performance gains depend on how well entropy production isolates true flow discontinuities, so detector tuning and robustness on different mesh/physics regimes remain important.
infographic.paper_title: eMOOD: Entropy-Based Multidimensional Optimal Order Detection for High-Order Shock-Capturing Finite-Volume Schemes

title: Active Sculpting: morphodynamics of internally stirred active vesicles
authors: Devadevan M M, Brato Chakrabarti
abstract: Active flows are often confined by soft, deformable boundaries that they can push against, reshape, and in turn get reorganized by. Motivated by this interplay, we combine theory and numerical simulations to analyze the morphodynamics of an elastic vesicle enclosing a dilute suspension of extensile active particles. We model the two-dimensional vesicle as a weakly extensible elastic ring with bending rigidity, immersed in a Stokesian fluid, and describe the confined active suspension using a kinetic theory. The vesicle and the suspension are coupled hydrodynamically, through the kinematic and dynamic boundary conditions at the interface, and energetically, through a single alignment interaction that simultaneously aligns active particles with the membrane and the membrane with the particles. We show that this interaction reduces to a weak-anchoring boundary condition familiar from passive liquid crystals and derive a closed-form quiescent equilibrium state in which the nematic order in the suspension organizes into a vortex with a +1 defect core. A stability analysis of this state predicts an ordered hierarchy of activity thresholds at which successive shape modes of the vesicle are destabilized, as well as a purely passive, anchoring-driven instability of floppy vesicles. Nonlinear simulations, performed with a volume-conserving immersed boundary method, reveal that each threshold crossing gives rise to a distinct emergent state: a static spindle with boundary-pinned defects, a rotor that tank treads against its own rotation, a fluctuating spinner, and a turbulent state in which the vesicle acts as a self-stirring compartment. Beyond demonstrating how boundary deformability sculpts, and is sculpted by, confined active matter, our results open the door to study hydrodynamic interactions between such active vesicles and to use membrane fluctuations as a probe of activity of suspensions.

infographic.key_insight: Internally stirred active particles and a deformable elastic vesicle co-evolve: activity reorganizes the membrane, while membrane softness and anchoring reshape the collective flow, producing distinct shape-and-dynamics transitions as activity increases.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This work informs the design of soft, active microcontainers and synthetic cells by showing how boundary mechanics can tune mixing, transport, and flow states in confined active suspensions.
method: 2D weakly extensible elastic-ring model with bending rigidity in Stokes flow
Kinetic theory for a dilute extensile active-particle suspension coupled to the vesicle by hydrodynamic and alignment interactions
Stability analysis plus nonlinear volume-conserving immersed-boundary simulations
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports analytical stability thresholds and simulation results that identify successive morphodynamic states: spindle, rotor, fluctuating spinner, and turbulent self-stirring behavior.
infographic.watch_item: The study is a 2D model with weak-anchoring assumptions and dilute suspension kinetics, so quantitative behavior may change for 3D vesicles, stronger coupling, or denser active matter.
infographic.paper_title: Active Sculpting: morphodynamics of internally stirred active vesicles

title: Partially-Averaged Navier-Stokes simulation of turbulent annular Poiseulle flow
authors: Li-Toong Yap, Marten Klein, Heiko Schmidt
abstract: Turbulent annular Poiseulle flow is commonly encountered in various engineering applications, such as heat exchangers. The effects of the inner wall transverse curvature on the flowfield, characterised by the ratio of inner and outer radii $η= R_{i}/R_{o}$, have been studied previously using Direct Numerical Simulations (DNS). Scale-resolving simulations based on a Reynolds-Averaged Navier Stokes framework offer a potentially cheaper alternative to traditional Large Eddy Simulations (LES); however it is not clear if such models are able to capture the turbulence anisotropy in the turbulent annular pipe flow. In the present study, turbulent annular Poiseulle flow at $Re_{D_{h}} = 8900$ is performed with the Partially-Averaged Navier Stokes (PANS) model, a variable-resolution turbulence model that is based on the conventional RANS modelling. The ability of the PANS model to capture the effects of the transverse wall curvature is found to be comparable with DNS and other RANS-based scale-resolving approaches despite its relative simplicity and reduced computational cost.

infographic.key_insight: A PANS simulation can capture the curvature-driven turbulence behavior in annular Poiseuille flow with accuracy comparable to DNS and other RANS-based scale-resolving methods.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests a lower-cost modeling route for heat-exchanger and annular duct designs where inner-wall curvature strongly affects turbulent transport.
method: Simulated turbulent annular Poiseuille flow using the Partially-Averaged Navier-Stokes (PANS) model
Studied the effect of transverse wall curvature via the radius ratio η = Ri/Ro
Benchmarked performance at ReDh = 8900 against DNS and other RANS-based scale-resolving approaches
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that PANS reproduces curvature effects in the flowfield with performance comparable to DNS and similar scale-resolving methods.
infographic.watch_item: The result is shown for a single Reynolds number and geometry range, so broader validation is needed before generalizing to other annular-flow conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Partially-Averaged Navier-Stokes simulation of turbulent annular Poiseulle flow

title: Response of Confined Mesoscale Flames to Acoustic Forcing
authors: Akhil Aravind, Balasundaram Mohan, Saptarshi Basu
abstract: Mesoscale combustion plays a vital role in applications ranging from portable power generation to micro-propulsion systems. This study investigates the response of mesoscale flames to upstream acoustic forcing across three characteristic flame regimes: Flames with Repetitive Extinction and Ignition (FREI), Stable Flames (SF), and Propagating Flames (PF). Acoustic forcing is applied over a broad range of pressure intensities at the first harmonic of the combustor tube. At low forcing intensities, all the flame regimes exhibit oscillations at the forcing frequency without qualitative changes in their respective flame behaviours. However, as the acoustic pressure increases, all flame regimes transition to a common unsteady regime characterised by periodic ignition-extinction cycles (resembling FREI) alongside strong oscillations at the forcing frequency. This response is identified as the oscillating FREI (O-FREI) regime, in which increasing forcing intensity leads to a reduction in the mean heat release rate, an amplification of oscillations at the forcing frequency, and a drop in the Strouhal number associated with the ignition-extinction cycle. The response characteristics across all flame regimes are examined in detail and are further complemented using reduced-order mathematical models.

infographic.key_insight: Upstream acoustic forcing drives all three mesoscale flame regimes into a common oscillating FREI (O-FREI) state, where stronger forcing increases forcing-frequency oscillations while reducing mean heat release and the ignition-extinction Strouhal number.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results help predict and manage combustion stability in confined mesoscale devices such as portable power systems and micro-propulsion combustors under acoustic disturbances.
method: Tested three flame regimes: FREI, stable flames (SF), and propagating flames (PF).
Applied upstream acoustic forcing at the combustor tube’s first harmonic over a broad range of pressure intensities.
Used reduced-order mathematical models to complement and interpret the observed flame responses.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports regime-dependent observations across a broad range of forcing intensities, showing a transition at higher acoustic pressures to a shared O-FREI behavior.
infographic.watch_item: The findings are based on a specific confined mesoscale combustor and first-harmonic forcing, so broader applicability to other geometries or forcing spectra should be validated.
infographic.paper_title: Response of Confined Mesoscale Flames to Acoustic Forcing

title: CFD Forge: A Physics-Constrained Agentic Framework for Autonomous CFD
authors: Aakash Shailesh Oza, Ryan F. Johnson, Amir Barati Farimani
abstract: Setting up, running, and assessing a computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulation requires substantial manual effort, from meshing and solver setup to diagnosis and interpretation, and repeating it across design variants slows engineering iteration. We present CFD Forge, an agentic framework built around OpenFOAM that carries an engineering request through case construction, meshing, solver execution, diagnostics, and reporting. A large language model interprets the request, reads the simulation evidence, identifies likely causes of problems, and proposes actions from a closed set. Automation is only useful if its results can be trusted, so acceptance is not left to the model: deterministic checks, registered for each type of flow, measure explicit criteria and decide. We demonstrate the framework on a converging-diverging nozzle and a two-dimensional forward-facing step, including geometry and operating changes requested in text. A turbulent cube, run outside the agent loop, shows why the checks matter: the solver completed and the mean drag settled, but the lateral-force oscillations were still growing, so a retrospective assessment withheld acceptance. To test this separation, we replayed 36 recorded simulation states, some with deliberately altered diagnostics, through the same model in two setups. Judging from the evidence without the check results, the model accepted 12 of the 13 detectable faults in all three repeats; with CFD Forge's checks deciding, none was accepted. The two setups also differ in prompting, and a fixed rule reached the same verdicts, so the model's value lies in the open-ended work rather than the verdict. Case files, recorded model calls, and decisions are retained for audit. A model that does the work, paired with checks that decide what is accepted, is a step toward automated CFD that can be trusted in high-throughput design and active-learning loops.

infographic.key_insight: CFD Forge automates CFD case setup, execution, diagnosis, and reporting with an LLM, but uses deterministic physics checks—not the model—to decide whether results are accepted.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables faster, more repeatable CFD workflows for design iteration and high-throughput studies while keeping acceptance decisions auditable and trustworthy.
method: LLM interprets the engineering request and proposes actions from a closed set.
OpenFOAM-based agent carries the case through geometry/case construction, meshing, solver execution, diagnostics, and reporting.
Registered deterministic checks evaluate flow-specific criteria and determine acceptance independently of the model.
infographic.evidence_signal: In 36 replayed simulation states with some altered diagnostics, the model accepted 12 of 13 detectable faults when judging without checks, but accepted none when CFD Forge’s checks controlled the verdicts.
infographic.watch_item: The framework depends on well-designed registered checks and robust diagnostics; if the checks are incomplete, failure modes may still slip through.
infographic.paper_title: CFD Forge: A Physics-Constrained Agentic Framework for Autonomous CFD

title: Wave-driven geostrophic vortices in rotating turbulence
authors: Vladimir Parfenyev, Sergey Vergeles
abstract: We perform direct numerical simulations of rotating turbulence to investigate the mechanisms responsible for the maintenance of large-scale geostrophic vortices. We confirm that the Reynolds stresses generated by inertial waves are consistent with the Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes balance of the large-scale flow and demonstrate the predicted cyclone-anticyclone asymmetry, with cyclones exhibiting stronger azimuthal velocities and more compact cores. Wave-field analysis provides evidence that geostrophic vortices selectively reflect and absorb inertial waves according to the sign of their angular momentum. Wave absorption occurs either through the formation of a critical layer ahead of the reflection point or through enhanced viscous dissipation associated with increasing local wavenumber. As rotation increases, fewer inertial waves undergo resonant absorption, reducing angular-momentum transfer to the vortices and weakening the geostrophic flow. Consequently, the fraction of energy contained in geostrophic modes depends non-monotonically on the rotation rate, demonstrating that sufficiently rapid rotation can ultimately suppress, rather than enhance, turbulence two-dimensionalization.

infographic.key_insight: In rotating turbulence, large-scale geostrophic vortices are sustained by inertial-wave Reynolds stresses, and their growth depends on selective wave reflection and absorption that favors one vortex sign over the other.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These results help predict when strong rotation will amplify or suppress large-scale coherent vortices in geophysical and rotating-fluid systems, informing models of turbulence transport and momentum redistribution.
method: Direct numerical simulations of rotating turbulence
Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes balance analysis for the large-scale flow
Inertial-wave field analysis to identify reflection, critical layers, and viscous absorption
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports DNS evidence that wave-generated Reynolds stresses match the large-scale RANS balance and reproduce cyclone-anticyclone asymmetry, with geostrophic energy varying non-monotonically with rotation rate.
infographic.watch_item: The mechanism depends on resonant wave absorption, so predictions may change if the flow conditions or numerical resolution alter wave–vortex interactions or dissipation pathways.
infographic.paper_title: Wave-driven geostrophic vortices in rotating turbulence

title: Preferential concentration in a periodically forced particle-laden turbulent planar jet
authors: Mohammad Ahmad, Pierre Bragança, Christophe Cuvier, Martin Obligado
abstract: Periodic forcing is common in particle-laden jets, yet its influence on turbulence and inertial-particle clustering remains poorly understood. We investigate a turbulent planar jet at two Reynolds numbers, approximately 4950 and 9900 based on nozzle height, subjected to sinusoidal forcing at a frequency three orders of magnitude below the preferred jet instability. Hot-wire anemometry and high-speed particle imaging characterise the carrier turbulence, while Voronoi tessellations quantify preferential concentration of dilute inertial droplets. Despite its low frequency and moderate amplitude, forcing substantially modifies turbulence while leaving the mean-flow development nearly unchanged. The integral scale decreases by up to $40\%$, while forced and unforced jets retain the same time-averaged relationship between the dimensionless dissipation coefficient and Taylor-scale Reynolds number. Within the forcing cycle, velocity fluctuations and the Taylor microscale vary approximately in opposite phase, keeping the Taylor-scale Reynolds number within $\pm10\%$ of its cycle mean despite substantial variations in dissipation and Kolmogorov time scale. Particle clustering is even more sensitive, with forcing increasing mean preferential concentration and producing phase-dependent variations of $21$--$49\%$ of the cycle mean. Clustering peaks when the Kolmogorov time scale is largest, corresponding to the smallest particle Stokes number. Thus, markedly different clustering states occur at similar instantaneous Taylor-scale Reynolds numbers. These findings demonstrate that weak temporal modulation can control particle organisation without substantially altering the mean transporting flow.

infographic.key_insight: Weak, low-frequency sinusoidal forcing can substantially reshape turbulence and increase inertial-particle clustering in a planar jet, even though the mean flow changes little.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Periodic modulation offers a potential control knob for particle distribution and mixing in jets, with implications for sprays, combustion, and particulate transport systems.
method: Hot-wire anemometry measured carrier-flow turbulence at two Reynolds numbers.
High-speed particle imaging and Voronoi tessellation quantified preferential concentration of dilute inertial droplets.
Forced and unforced jets were compared over the forcing cycle to relate turbulence scales, Stokes number, and clustering.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across two Reynolds numbers, forcing reduced the integral scale by up to 40% and increased preferential concentration, with phase-dependent clustering variations of 21–49% of the cycle mean.
infographic.watch_item: The study is specific to weak periodic forcing in a planar jet, so the observed clustering control may not transfer directly to other geometries, forcing amplitudes, or particle loading regimes.
infographic.paper_title: Preferential concentration in a periodically forced particle-laden turbulent planar jet

title: GeONet: Geometry-Encoded Operator Network for Predicting Flow in Heterogeneous Porous Media
authors: Md Lal Mamud, Maruti K. Mudunuru, Yucheng Fu, Aramy Troung, Satish Karra, Ivani Patel
abstract: Rapid prediction of pressure-driven flow in microfluidic porous media is important for experimental design, tracer-test interpretation, and digital-twin development for subsurface energy and critical mineral applications. High-fidelity simulations resolve geometry-controlled flow but are computationally expensive across large geometry ensembles. Here, we introduce GeONet, a Geometry-Encoded Operator Network that predicts steady-state pressure fields by jointly representing material properties, spatial coordinates, and solid--void geometry. GeONet extends the Branch--Trunk architecture with a dedicated Leaf Network encoding the binary domain mask through multiscale features. The Branch Network represents porosity and permeability, the Trunk Network combines coordinates with local geometric descriptors and random Fourier features, and a gated DeepMixer integrates these representations to predict pressure. GeONet was trained and evaluated using 5,000 PFLOTRAN simulations of heterogeneous Reduced Complexity Platform domains, comprising nearly 30 TB of data. Comparisons with pore-scale Stokes solutions across three geometries yielded Pearson correlations of 0.987--0.991 and $R^2$ values of 0.974--0.982, supporting PFLOTRAN as reference data. Under matched partitions and two-stage hyperparameter optimization, GeONet substantially outperformed a boundary-condition-aware DeepONet baseline. Across three held-out domains, GeONet achieved NRMSE of 0.0381--0.0500, MAPE of 1.76--2.59%, and $R^2$ of 0.9673--0.9822, versus 0.1483--0.2040, 7.81--10.45%, and 0.5658--0.7126 for DeepONet, respectively. On three additional unseen geometries, GeONet achieved NRMSE of 0.0448--0.0676 and $R^2$ of 0.9511--0.9770. These results demonstrate improved accuracy, pressure-range preservation, and cross-geometry generalization through explicit geometry encoding.

infographic.key_insight: GeONet improves flow-field prediction in porous media by explicitly encoding geometry alongside material properties and coordinates, enabling stronger cross-geometry generalization than a DeepONet baseline.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model can accelerate pressure-field prediction for microfluidic experiments, tracer-test interpretation, and digital-twin workflows where many heterogeneous pore geometries must be evaluated quickly.
method: Extends the Branch-Trunk operator network with a Leaf Network that encodes the binary solid-void mask.
Uses porosity, permeability, coordinates, and local geometric descriptors with random Fourier features.
Fuses representations with a gated DeepMixer to predict steady-state pressure.
infographic.evidence_signal: Trained on 5,000 PFLOTRAN simulations (~30 TB) and evaluated on held-out and unseen geometries, GeONet achieved NRMSE of 0.0381–0.0676 and R2 of 0.9511–0.9822, substantially outperforming DeepONet.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on high-quality geometry masks and large simulation datasets, so deployment may be limited when geometry encoding is noisy or training coverage is sparse.
infographic.paper_title: GeONet: Geometry-Encoded Operator Network for Predicting Flow in Heterogeneous Porous Media

title: On the relationships between pressure geometrization and vortex identification
authors: Han Tu, Hang Zhao, Qi Gao
abstract: The profound mathematical and conceptual analogy between pressure in fluid mechanics and gravity in general relativity motivates a novel geometric reinterpretation of flows. This article proposes a theoretical framework for geometrizing pressure by establishing a Newton-Cartan geometry and applying a conformal transformation to the spatial metric. The pressure field is reinterpreted as a geometric potential that induces an effective spatial curvature, encoded in the Ricci tensor Rij and the associated Einstein-like tensor Gij. Within this curved effective space, fluid particles under the exclusive influence of pressure follow geodesics, and the classical Euler equation is recovered in the weak-field limit. The pressure Poisson equation emerges naturally as a consequence of the geodesic equation and the Bianchi identity, revealing pressure as an instantaneous geometric constraint rather than an external force. This framework provides a unified geometric interpretation of widely used vortex identification criteria, demonstrating that the prevailing Eulerian and Lagrangian schemes correspond to different geometric invariants or projections of the effective curvature. In the degenerate two-dimensional (2D) limit, the effective spatial tensor vanishes identically, and the global integral of the total curvature vanishes as well. This topological constraint offers a novel interpretation of the dual-cascade scenario in 2D turbulence: the inverse energy cascade arises from geometric condensation of positive-curvature structures toward larger scales, while the forward enstrophy cascade results from geometric dispersion of negative-curvature structures toward smaller scales.

infographic.key_insight: The paper reframes pressure as a geometric potential that curves an effective space, unifying pressure-driven motion and vortex identification through curvature-based invariants.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives fluid engineers a new physics-based lens for interpreting vortices, pressure fields, and 2D turbulence cascades in CFD and flow diagnostics.
method: Build a Newton-Cartan geometric framework for pressure.
Apply a conformal transformation to define an effective curved spatial metric.
Relate vortex criteria to Ricci/Einstein-like curvature invariants and geodesic motion.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract presents a theoretical derivation rather than a data-driven benchmark, showing consistency with the Euler equation, the pressure Poisson equation, and 2D topological constraints.
infographic.watch_item: The framework is largely conceptual and geometric, so practical use will depend on how robustly the curvature quantities can be computed from noisy experimental or simulation data.
infographic.paper_title: On the relationships between pressure geometrization and vortex identification

title: High-Frequency Mass Transfer Enabling Over-Limiting Currents in Porous Electrodes
authors: Md Abdul Hamid, Kyle C. Smith
abstract: Classical film theory predicts a finite diffusion-limited current at porous electrodes. However, over-limiting currents (OLCs), which exceed this limit, are often observed and have been attributed to surface charge, confinement, or electrokinetic effects. Here, we use a frequency-domain framework to identify a different mechanism governed by the time scale of concentration variation. For perfectly reactive interfaces, the spectral Sherwood number, a frequency-dependent dimensionless measure of interfacial mass transfer relative to molecular diffusion, grows as $\Shnd\simω^{1/2}$ at high frequency, while its phase approaches $π/4$. This response corresponds to the semi-infinite Warburg limit of the electrochemical impedance. A scaling analysis shows that the exponent and prefactor are determined by diffusion within a thin layer adjacent to the interface and are therefore independent of the global pore geometry. Numerical results for parallel plates, circular tubes, and twelve porous microstructures confirm this scaling. Geometry, flow strength, and flow direction affect the low-frequency response and crossover frequency, but not the asymptotic scaling in the high-frequency limit. This temporal route to OLCs requires neither surface charge nor confinement and could inform the design of systems for pulsed electrodeposition, mineral recovery and renewable-energy storage.

infographic.key_insight: High-frequency concentration oscillations near a reactive porous electrode create a diffusion-layer-controlled mass transfer boost, giving a universal \u03a9^{1/2}-type over-limiting current response.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests pulsed electrochemical systems can exceed classical diffusion limits without relying on surface charge or confinement, which is useful for electrodeposition, mineral recovery, and energy storage.
method: Frequency-domain mass-transfer analysis with spectral Sherwood number
Asymptotic scaling for the high-frequency Warburg limit
Numerical tests on parallel plates, circular tubes, and 12 porous microstructures
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical confirmation across multiple geometries and flow conditions, showing geometry affects low-frequency behavior and crossover but not the high-frequency \u03a9^{1/2} scaling.
infographic.watch_item: The asymptotic over-limiting behavior is a high-frequency limit result, so real devices must still ensure pulse frequencies and diffusion-layer conditions match the modeled regime.
infographic.paper_title: High-Frequency Mass Transfer Enabling Over-Limiting Currents in Porous Electrodes

title: Kinetic Equations and Turbulence in Large $N$ Vector and SYK-like Models
authors: Vladimir Rosenhaus, Daniel Schubring
abstract: We apply large $N$ expansion techniques to derive kinetic equations for strongly coupled, far-from-equilibrium field theories with $O(N)$ symmetry. For large $N$ vector models, the quasi-classical approximation holds. Incorporating arbitrary momentum-dependent interactions, we show the dynamics obey the standard kinetic equation, with the scattering amplitude given by the retarded propagator of the auxiliary Hubbard-Stratonovich field. This has broad applications to systems like spin wave and Langmuir ion-acoustic turbulence. For large $N$ random coupling (SYK-like) models in $d$ dimensions, leading-order melon diagrams induce order-one propagator renormalization and finite spectral width. The corresponding kinetic equation, unlike those for standard weakly interacting systems, does not have a local-in-time collision integral. We find evidence for a stationary, scale-invariant infrared solution, revealing a potentially novel strong turbulence scaling exponent.

infographic.key_insight: Large-$N$ field theories can be reduced to kinetic equations, but SYK-like random-coupling models generate nonlocal collision dynamics and a new strong-turbulence infrared scaling regime.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The result provides a principled framework for predicting transport and energy transfer in strongly coupled wave systems, with relevance to turbulence-like plasmas and collective excitations.
method: Use large-$N$ expansion to derive far-from-equilibrium kinetic equations.
For $O(N)$ vector models, identify the scattering amplitude with the retarded Hubbard-Stratonovich propagator.
For SYK-like models, include melon-diagram self-energy effects and analyze the resulting nonlocal collision term.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper reports analytical derivations and finds evidence for a stationary, scale-invariant infrared solution in the SYK-like case.
infographic.watch_item: The SYK-like kinetic equation lacks a local-in-time collision integral, so standard weak-turbulence intuitions and closures may fail.
infographic.paper_title: Kinetic Equations and Turbulence in Large $N$ Vector and SYK-like Models

title: Versatile two-layer model for thermohydraulic prediction of microchannel heat sinks
authors: Chih-Hsiang Chen, Kentaro Yaji
abstract: Three-dimensional conjugate heat-transfer simulations provide detailed predictions for microchannel heat sinks but can be computationally demanding when many geometries and operating conditions are evaluated. This study develops a versatile two-layer model (VTLM) that reduces the three-dimensional problem to two coupled two-dimensional fields while retaining the in-plane geometry of the flow passages and fins. Effects associated with the unresolved channel-height direction are incorporated through hydraulic and thermal closures that account for wall friction and the fluid- and fin-side contributions to interlayer heat transfer. The closures are evaluated from the representative channel geometry, flow-development condition, and fin configuration. The VTLM was assessed against three-dimensional reference models across broad ranges of channel aspect ratios and operating conditions, including uniform and nonuniform fin arrangements. Compared with the existing two-layer models, the VTLM showed improved overall agreement with the three-dimensional reference results. The results showed that prediction accuracy was governed mainly by the flow-development condition and channel aspect ratio, from which a conservative screening guideline was proposed for the examined straight-channel configurations. The assessment of finned expansion--contraction channels further supported the applicability of the VTLM to the investigated passages with abrupt width changes. Overall, the VTLM provides a reduced-dimensional framework for thermohydraulic analysis across the range of microchannel heat-sink configurations examined in this study without explicitly resolving the channel-height direction.

infographic.key_insight: A versatile two-layer model (VTLM) compresses 3D microchannel heat-sink conjugate heat transfer into two coupled 2D fields while preserving in-plane geometry and improving agreement with full 3D predictions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: VTLM offers a faster reduced-order tool for screening microchannel heat-sink designs and operating conditions without explicitly resolving the channel-height direction.
method: Couples two 2D fields to represent fluid and fin regions in place of a full 3D model.
Uses hydraulic and thermal closure relations to capture wall friction and interlayer heat transfer.
Derives closures from representative channel geometry, flow development, and fin configuration.
infographic.evidence_signal: The model was benchmarked against 3D reference simulations over broad ranges of channel aspect ratios, operating conditions, and both uniform and nonuniform fin arrangements, and it outperformed existing two-layer models overall.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy depends strongly on flow-development condition and channel aspect ratio, so the proposed screening guideline should be applied cautiously outside the examined straight-channel and expansion-contraction cases.
infographic.paper_title: Versatile two-layer model for thermohydraulic prediction of microchannel heat sinks
